newsitem.title: BELGIUM: French socialist says party would seek EMU talks.
newsitem.headline: French socialist says party would seek EMU talks.

text.p: The moment it took office, a French Socialist government would ask for talks with other European Union countries about the single currency, a leading member of the party said on Thursday.

"We take power in one month. We call for a discussion with our partners," Elizabeth Guigou, a Socialist Euro-MP who was France's negotiator leading up to the Maastricht Treaty, said in an interview with a small group of reporters.
The discussion would focus on the way the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria are being interpreted, the former European affairs minister said.
Gigou said that the criteria -- which includes forcing deficits down to three percent of Gross Domestic Product -- had become a "fetish".
"The treaty says they are reference points," she said. "We would not pick the same figures today."

France has called for elections on May 25. Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has sounded a sceptical note about the criteria, but Gigou appeared to go much further -- including calling for the renegotiation of the post-EMU stability pact agreed by EU leaders in December.
She challenged current policy in France, Germany and at the European Commission that to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, deficits must not be higher that three percent of GDP.
To force countries like Germany and France to respect this limit meant they had to carry out extra budgetary measures.
"If we continue this infernal spiral of budgetary rigour, we will never attain our potential for growth and never succeed in reducing unemployment," she said.
"It's a death wish which is going to throw Europe into recession and deflation," Gigou said.
She said a Socialist government would want to renegotiate the stability pact agreed at the Dublin EU summit as a way of ensuring discipline after the single currency is introduced.
"A single currency which translated into perpetual austerity would be a currency set to collapse," she said.
What was needed was an "economic government" to run parrallel with the European Central Bank in order to discuss the dollar/euro exchange rate and the coordination of economic policy.
Guigou said she believed it was possible to persuade Bonn to accept such changes if France offered German Chancellor Helmut Kohl true political union.
